lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fabio Luiz Segura | Lesson 18 -- The Bradesco Pitch Evolved

listenings.text: Let me start with a question. How long does it take you to pay a supplier in another country? For most of the small exporters we work with in Chile, the honest answer is too long. My name is Laura, and I lead the trade innovation team at a mid-sized bank in Santiago. We have worked with exporters for more than thirty years. Here is the problem. Inside Chile, a payment takes seconds. But when one of our small exporters sells to Brazil or to the United States, they can wait up to twelve days to get paid. Twelve days is the difference between growing and borrowing. What we are really trying to solve for is that gap. We have been running a pilot in one corridor, and the same payment now takes about twelve minutes. Twelve days to twelve minutes. So that is actually what I would love to explore with someone like you. Do you have thirty minutes for a coffee tomorrow? We could compare our corridors and see if one pilot makes sense for both sides.

The most common mistake I see in a short pitch is energy. People start with all of it. The first sentence is loud and fast, and by the end they have nothing left, which is a shame, because the end is where the request is. So try it the other way round. Make your first sentence a little slower and a little lower than normal. It sounds calm, and it makes people lean in. Then let the energy build through the problem and the solution. That is where your numbers are, so let them be louder. And when you get to the invitation, let your voice go up and then come down gently at the end. That movement sounds like an open door. A flat, falling voice sounds like the end of a speech, and nobody replies to the end of a speech.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the first sentence or question that catches the listener's attention
a short fact about you or your work that makes the listener trust what you say
to begin a pitch or a conversation with a question instead of a statement
a very short presentation of who you are and what you offer, short enough for an elevator ride
a memorable idea in your pitch that the other person can come back to later
a clear request at the end that tells the listener what to do next
the shape of a story, from the beginning through the tension to the end
one sentence that says what you do, for whom, and why you are different

paras: Most conference pitches are not bad. They are incomplete. The speaker explains the bank, the department and the product well, and then stops, one step before the only part that produces a result. The listener says very interesting, takes a card, and nothing happens. A good pitch is not a presentation of what you have. It is a short narrative arc that ends with a conversation you want to have.

The arc has four parts. The first is context: who you are and why the listener should trust you. Keep it short. One positioning statement and one credibility marker are enough, for example twenty years in trade finance or the size of your bank. Experienced people often spend half their time here, because it is the part they know best. It is also the part the listener cares about least.

The second part is the problem, and it needs one number. Not a list of challenges, but one gap the listener can picture. The third is your angle: what your area is exploring to close that gap. This is where a pilot, a result or a conversation anchor belongs, one memorable idea the other person can come back to later at dinner. Many good speakers lead with a question here, or even at the very start, because a question is the best hook there is.

The fourth part is the one most pitches forget: the invitation. It is a call to action, but a soft one. You are not closing a deal in three minutes. You are trying to open a door, so the request should be small and concrete: thirty minutes tomorrow, a call next week, one corridor to compare.

Finally, stop. An elevator pitch takes thirty seconds and a full pitch takes three minutes, not ten. If the other person has questions, that is good news. The goal is to leave them wanting more, so that the next conversation is their idea.
